_note: Gold eval set for thesis ANSWER quality. Each item is one question put to the decision engine, with the thesis + aspect it belongs to and what a strong, purpose-driven answer must cover. Scored by eval/judge.py. Extend freely; keep it small and representative across domains and aspect kinds (corpus-settleable vs call_only, factual vs comparative).

items.thesis: Cerebras will win wafer-scale AI inference customers away from Nvidia GPUs in 2025.
items.question: Are named customers actually moving production inference workloads to Cerebras instead of Nvidia?
items.target: Named enterprises run production inference on Cerebras rather than Nvidia GPUs.
items.rubric_focus: Should name specific customers (e.g. a labeled foundation-model lab or enterprise), cite concrete throughput/contract figures, and distinguish signed/announced from realized deployment. A pass is specific and cited; a fail is generic 'some firms are interested'.

items.thesis: Incumbent CRM vendors are differentiating on AI agents, reshaping mid-market vendor selection.
items.question: What are the major CRM vendors today, how do they differentiate, and how are they adapting to AI agents?
items.target: Major CRM vendors differ on product and are adapting to AI agents in distinct ways.
items.rubric_focus: A strong answer is a COMPARISON across several named vendors (Salesforce, Microsoft, HubSpot, etc.) on differentiator + agent play, cited. A wall of prose or a single-vendor answer is weak.

items.thesis: RBAC is inadequate for AI-agent access control, opening a market for agent-native authorization.
items.question: Do practitioners and the record show that RBAC is insufficient for AI-agent access control?
items.target: RBAC is insufficient for governing AI-agent access.
items.rubric_focus: Should give the concrete failure mechanism (static roles vs variable agent scope, machine-speed, over-broad permissions) with cited sources, not a vague 'RBAC has limits'.

items.thesis: Mid-market 3PL warehouses will pay for fixed ceiling-mounted computer-vision cameras to replace handheld barcode scanners.
items.question: Does willingness to pay for camera-based inventory tracking exceed the cost to serve for mid-market 3PLs?
items.target: Mid-market 3PLs will pay more for camera inventory tracking than it costs to serve them.
items.rubric_focus: This is call_only. A strong answer surfaces what the record DOES show (labor-cost proxies, incumbent pricing) AND is explicit that a filed budget for an unoffered SKU cannot settle it — it needs a buyer call. It must NOT fabricate a willingness-to-pay number, and must not bare-'not established'.

items.thesis: Open-source LLMs will win the enterprise on total cost of ownership.
items.question: Is there a catalyst forcing enterprises to revisit closed vs open LLMs on cost now?
items.target: A recent catalyst is pushing enterprises to reconsider open-source LLMs on cost.
items.rubric_focus: Should name a concrete, recent catalyst (a price change, a capability parity milestone, a compliance shift) with a date and a cited source, not a timeless 'costs matter'.

items.thesis: Vertical AI drafting copilots will win law firms away from horizontal LLM assistants.
items.question: Is there an existing budget line at law firms that a vertical AI drafting copilot is bought from, and who owns it?
items.target: Law firms have a budget category that a vertical AI drafting copilot is purchased from.
items.rubric_focus: Name the actual budget line (legal-tech / knowledge-management / practice-innovation), name owners or named-vendor deployments at named firms, cited. Vague 'firms are adopting AI' is weak.

items.thesis: Databricks will out-grow Snowflake in enterprise data-and-AI platform spend.
items.question: How do Databricks and Snowflake compare on enterprise adoption, growth, and AI-workload traction?
items.target: Databricks is gaining enterprise data-and-AI platform share against Snowflake.
items.rubric_focus: A COMPARISON with named metrics (revenue/growth, customer counts, named enterprise wins, AI product traction) and cited sources, distinguishing announced from realized. A single-vendor gloss is weak.

items.thesis: Stablecoins are becoming the default rail for cross-border B2B payments.
items.question: Does the status quo of correspondent-bank cross-border B2B payments cost real money and time that stablecoins remove?
items.target: Correspondent-bank cross-border B2B payments cost material fees and settlement time.
items.rubric_focus: Concrete cost/time figures for the status quo (fee %, settlement days) AND evidence of realized stablecoin B2B volume with dates, cited; distinguish pilots from production. Timeless 'payments are slow' is weak.

items.thesis: Mid-market MSSPs will move tier-1 SOC triage to AI copilots.
items.question: Is it feasible for a mid-market MSSP to switch tier-1 SOC triage from analysts to an AI copilot?
items.target: A mid-market MSSP can surmount the cost of switching tier-1 triage to an AI copilot.
items.rubric_focus: call_only: surface integration/trust/workflow-change proxies from the record and be explicit that switching EASE needs an operator call; must not fabricate adoption or bare-'not established'.

items.thesis: Infra SaaS is shifting from seat-based to usage-based pricing.
items.question: Is there a recent catalyst pushing infra SaaS vendors from seat-based to usage-based pricing now?
items.target: A recent catalyst is driving infra SaaS toward usage-based pricing.
items.rubric_focus: Name specific recent pricing-model changes by named vendors with dates and cited sources; a timeless 'usage pricing is popular' is weak.

items.thesis: Humanoid robots will reach commercial product-market fit in warehouse picking before manufacturing.
items.question: Are humanoid robots actually being deployed for warehouse picking today, beyond demos?
items.target: Humanoid robots are in real warehouse-picking deployments, not just demos.
items.rubric_focus: Name specific robots/vendors and warehouse deployments with concrete task/throughput, and clearly separate pilots/demos from paid production. Generic 'robots are coming' is weak.

items.thesis: Nvidia's CUDA software moat is eroding as inference shifts to alternative accelerators.
items.question: Is there evidence that production inference is moving to non-Nvidia accelerators despite CUDA lock-in?
items.target: Production inference workloads are running on non-Nvidia accelerators despite CUDA.
items.rubric_focus: Name specific alternative accelerators, named production deployments, and portability tooling/frameworks, cited; distinguish benchmark claims from realized migration. Vague 'competition is heating up' is weak.
